sentences.text: Russellosaurus was a small mosasauroid with a light build and a narrow frontal bone featuring a length-to-width ratio of 1.6:1.
Its skull possessed sixteen maxillary teeth and sixteen dentary teeth.
The anterior premaxilla is broad and blunt, displaying an oblique premaxillary-maxillary suture when viewed from above.
The frontal bone shows incipient emargination caused by the external nares.
The pineal foramen is located in the center of the triangular parietal table.
The type specimen is notable as the oldest well-preserved mosasaur found in North America.
It is the second mosasaur species named after Dale A. Russell, following Selmasaurus russelli.
The genus was described from a skull found in the Arcadia Park Shale at Cedar Hill in Dallas County, Texas.
The type specimen, skull SMU 73056, was discovered in 1992 by a member of the Dallas Paleontological Society and donated to the Shuler Museum of Paleontology.
Fragmentary specimens have also been recovered from the Kamp Ranch Limestone at two other localities in the Dallas area.
Currently, only one fossil occurrence of Russellosaurus has been recorded in the database.
The holotype skull is believed to belong to a subadult individual based on the lack of basicranial fusion and high bone vascularization suggesting rapid growth.
This animal is classified within the family Mosasauridae.
The genus belongs to the subfamily Yaguarasaurinae.
Russellosaurus was designated the type genus of the new parafamily Russellosaurina, or subfamily Russellosaurinae.

The clade Russellosaurina includes mosasaurs more closely related to Tylosaurinae and Plioplatecarpinae than to Mosasaurinae, with Tethysaurus, Yaguarasaurus, and Russellosaurus forming its sister group.
The skull displays many diagnostic characters of Plioplatecarpinae while retaining many primitive traits.
The genus was named by Polcyn and Bell in 2005.
Fossils were found in the Arcadia Park Shale at Cedar Hill, Texas, dating to the early middle Turonian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
Russellosaurus lived during the Turonian stage, between 93.9 and 89.8 million years ago.
